New words formed by derivation carry stress on the second syllable, e.g. man-‘tabo ‘chair’ (PLACE-sit.down). Caac syllables typically have the structure V(C) (e.g. o ‘at; to’, âc ‘man’) or CV(C) (e.g. te ‘go down’, pum ‘smoke’).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word; in words formed by derivation with a prefix (e.g. the place-nominalizer man-), stress stays on the first syllable of the root, i.e. surfaces on the second syllable of the derived word. Root-initial stress; no weight or length sensitivity mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: Derived words (prefix + root) are stressed on the second syllable, i.e. on the root's first syllable (man-'tabo 'chair'). No other exceptions given.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('Caac words'); cited forms are lexical citation forms including a possessed noun ('aremaa-n). Statement is one sentence in a phonological sketch inside a spatial-semantics thesis; no phonetic or instrumental support.
new_statements.identity_note: Cauchard 2014 describes present-day Caac of the Pouébo (Pweevo) area (villages Saint-Gabriel, Cabwen etc.), i.e. caac1237 proper. Hollyman 1962/1999 call the language 'Caaqac' and distinguish the Pouébo variety from the La Conception (Nouméa) diaspora variety 'Caawac' (no separate glottocode; Glottolog treats both under caac1237).

tone_statements.citation: Leenhardt, Maurice. 1946. Langues et dialectes de l'Austro-Mélanésie. (Travaux et mémoires de l'Institut d'ethnologie 46.) Paris: Institut d'ethnologie. xlviii+676 pp. [Notice 19 'Moenebeng' (région Pouébo), pp. 122-127; general 'Phonétique' pp. 4-11.]
tone_statements.quote: p. 122: « Les notes ci-dessous recueillies par un de nos aides indigènes, et non révisées (Cf. sup. Intr.) proviennent de la Conception. De nombreux indices montrent que la langue de ces immigrés a été contaminée. Trop de caractéristiques des langues du groupe sud apparaissent pour ne pas avertir que le vrai MOENEBENG reste encore à noter tout entier. » — p. 123: « § 2. — Accent et ton. a = nous [column 2:] ber = nous deux [line 2:] a = ils [column 2:] ber = eux deux » (complete content of the section). — p. 11 (general Phonétique, Conclusion): « Il reste à connaître l'accent, le ton, et les particularités phonétiques de chaque langue. On en trouvera le détail au chapitre réservé à chacune de celles-ci. » — p. 13 (Ajië, same section heading, the author's convention): « Deux syllabes ayant la même consonne et la même voyelle peuvent se distinguer par une différence de hauteur musicale. En indiquant par l'indice 1 le ton le plus bas, on note aisément quatre tons différents. xere¹ = nous, est bas xere³ = eux, est haut »
tone_statements.translation: p. 122: 'The notes below, collected by one of our native assistants and not revised (cf. Intr. above), come from La Conception. Many signs show that the language of these immigrants has been contaminated. Too many characteristics of the southern-group languages appear for us not to warn that the true Moenebeng still remains to be recorded in its entirety.' — p. 123: '§ 2. Accent and tone. a = we | ber = we two ; a = they | ber = they two.' — p. 11: 'The accent, the tone and the phonetic particularities of each language remain to be known. The detail will be found in the chapter reserved for each of them.' — p. 13 (Ajië): 'Two syllables having the same consonant and the same vowel can be distinguished by a difference of musical pitch. Marking the lowest tone with index 1, one easily notes four different tones. xere¹ = we, is low; xere³ = they, is high.'
tone_statements.locator: p. 123, 'I. Phonétique', '§ 2. — Accent et ton'; warning on the data p. 122; author's tone-notation convention p. 13 and p. 11
tone_statements.summary: No tone system described; a 1946 second-hand note implying a pitch ('hauteur musicale') contrast between 1st- and 3rd-person pronoun forms (a/a, ber/ber) in the La Conception (Caawac) variety of Caac, flagged by the author as southern-influenced; not evidence of lexical tone in Pouébo Caac.

sources.note: Full text not seen (Brill, restricted). The OpenAlex/INIST abstract is silent on tone: in the northern NC languages the evolution of POc *CVCV(C) canonical forms depends on word class (independent nouns/intransitives end in a closed syllable, inalienable nouns/transitives in an open one); archipelago-wide drift toward open final syllables with compensatory strengthening of the initial (pretonic-vowel loss giving geminates and pre/post-nasalised consonants, y-/kw- epenthesis, nasal spirants > nasal stops in the far south). No statement on Caac prosody is known.

sources.note: Full text not seen (JSTOR, restricted). The author's abstract (JSTOR RIS; French version in OpenAlex) is silent on tone: the northern languages are conservative in syllable structure (final consonants kept) but innovative in consonant place of articulation; the paper orders these changes chronologically and proposes a classification within the northern group, opening with canonical forms and consonant series. Caac data appear (p. 60 reflexes of POc *taku quoted by Cauchard 2014: 88 n.). Any remark on the absence of tone in the Far North is unverified.
